en: I dreamed of yearling-ewe fat frozen hard,
Kanykey, left by Manas,
Has not even a colt to ride.
I have suffered a great and dreadful hell!
Then Bölökbay stood and said:
“If we journey to Altai,
There is no thoroughbred, no racing steed;
Whom shall we make our swift mount?
The only one left by Manas is absent;
Whom shall we make our guiding light?
Kara-Zoo of Echkilik,
I have made my homeland as though it were level ground.
Semetey, left by Manas,
I have taken as my support, like his father.
With Kanykey thus departing in mourning,
Has Semetey escaped?
The six steels fallen from the sky,
Did the unfortunate one take them as a gift?
Fleeing Talas in concealment,
Has your unfortunate one survived?
Traveling up the valley,
Did they go along Kara-Üngkür?
In her advancing age,
Has Chyyyrdy also survived?
If he returned to Talas,
And we who grieve could see him,
Our hearts would be deeply content.
If we could see our orphan's eyes,
We would have no complaint against God.
Growing to maturity, becoming a man,
Will such a day come?
Becoming a lion like his father,
Will a day come when he returns to Talas?
From Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
Will a day come when he leads a migration?
Upon those dogs of evil aspect,
Semetey returning,
Will a day come when he takes revenge?
Think, dear elder Bakay:
For twelve years I shall yearn for the orphan.
Until my orphan reaches twelve,
This Kara-Tash here
I shall make my home!
For that one child, Semetey,
Elder Bakay, listen:
I shall press my soles upon the stone;
I shall shoot game and dry its meat.
The forty guards beside me,
My maimed ones, I shall keep safe.
If the departed orphan does not return,
The decree sent by Allah,
I shall know that this was it.
Of the orphan left by the generous hero,
Only then shall I give up hope.
My black beard turning white,
I shall grieve until I wither.
If Kanykey does not return,
On the day of the great gathering,
I shall make her a black donkey.
If the boy does not come in thirteen years,
I shall bite my finger and grieve.
When fourteen years are fulfilled,
I shall sorrow and turn my thoughts.
When fifteen years are fulfilled,
I shall slaughter the forty guards,
Elder Bakay, and die before my appointed death.
Elder Bakay, to let it be lost would bring a bad name.
I shall tell you a word in trust.
Your dear friend Kanykey
Was a dark-hearted soul.
Because of what had happened,
Because of the White Steed,
Kanykey toward her father
Had borne a grievance.
Tell her to put that grievance aside;
Tell her to end her troubled affairs!
Let her abandon narrow thoughts;
Without tiring, let Kanykey
Begin to think another way!
Tell her to agree to what he says;
Semetey in her keeping,
Tell her to give him to her brother Ismayyl.
Letting a swan be fed to a bird,
The child born from her womb,
Letting him be called another's son,
Tell her to raise him thus;
Tell her to please her father Karakan!
When he reaches five,
Let his valiant nature be known;
In Bukhara, the pillar of religion,
Let her send him into the mosque.
Until he reaches nine,
Let him learn the mullah's knowledge.
When he grows lively at ten,
Giving him a gun in his hand,
Let her make the boy an honored man.
When he reaches twelve,
Let her show him Talas again.
Until twelve years have passed,
I shall keep yearning for my orphan.
When my treasury was plundered,
Khan Manas's copper cauldron with forty handles,
Your dogs hacked it apart.
I shall repent before God.
For my orphan, if he returns,
I shall cast it anew as a good omen.
If my cauldron is restored,
I shall banish the sorrow within me.
A brown lamb remains in my keeping,
A lamb suckled by two mothers.
To sacrifice to Bahauddin,
I shall keep the brown lamb.
Until twelve years have passed,
I shall keep up my strength.
For the orphan left by my companion,
One that will not glance off stone,
I shall keep making a battle-axe.
Elder Bakay, speaking gives the heart contentment.
To take along as provisions,
The brown two-year-old wether in my keeping—
Apart from this, I have nothing at all.
Saying, ‘Bölökbay has been ruined,’
Elder Bakay, come and see me from time to time.
Let it feed him until he reaches great Bukhara;
Take the brown wether and give it to Semetey!”
When Bakay was about to ride away,
All forty guards,
Taking up their battle-axes and sobbing,
As though their own elder brother were leaving,
Saw the hero Bakay off.
“Tell them what we have said,” they said.
“Meet them and return,” they said.
They cried aloud in farewell.
Then Bakay the leopard
Turned his horse and galloped off.
Your swift one, Bakay the leopard,
Raced toward Kanykey.
With two fat horses,
With two skins of milk,
Openly breaking the course of events,
Uncle Bakay took the wether for provisions,
And set off toward Kara-Üngkür:
Such was Bakay’s lodging.
Of the flight to Bukhara,
Now let me tell you
The tale of your sister-in-law Kanykey.
Then Kanykey, left in mourning,
And Semetey were to flee.
With caves and mountains for her lodging,
There was Kanykey, sorely rebuffed.
Unable to bear staying in the cave,
Her trembling heart throbbing,
Unable to contain her sobs,
Her spirit cruelly torn,
Pines and bushes, stones and hills
All seemed like enemies.
Unable to endure three days in the cave,
Unable to lie and rest her life,
Unable to reach a settled destination,
Unable to muster herself and walk away,
Your mother wept and shrieked.
On one side the wild ram’s meat stank terribly,
The cave’s interior reeking;
Without eating the tainted meat,
On the other side Semetey cried and screamed.
“The only child obtained at death’s door
Will be left sick,” she said.
“God will take our lives in this way,” she said.
Your dear mother Chyyyrdy
Grieved on her side.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Bound and fastened once again,
Into the fold of her overskirt,
The child from the cradle,
Securing him firmly there.
Your capable mother Kanykey,
Revealing her widow’s plight,
Took powerless Chyyyrdy,
Her mother who had grown old,
Upon her moonlike back.
Walking straight ahead, her soul burned;
Unable to stand still, thirsty, her blood burned.
Unable to cross the ridge on foot,
Unable to reach a known place,
Unable to sleep on peaceful ground,
Your mother Kanykey
Could find no place upon the earth.
For two days in that isolated place
She went without lying down.
Two people upon one person
Went without room enough.
Her soles pounded against stone,
She grew thin as she went.
Wandering, weeping, walking on foot,
Your mother Kanykey went in misery.
Toward Temir Khan’s city
Your mother wandered, fleeing on foot;
Toward Karakan’s city
She walked on foot in grief.
Her joints weakened and wavered.
Her streaming tears
Glistened at her collarbone.
Her rib bones came apart;
The moonlike back that carried Chyyyrdy
Had flesh torn away in cupfuls.
With all her flanks rubbed raw,
Your sister-in-law, shrunk to a span,
Wounded every heart.
At every stride, without respite,
The flesh of her soles crumbled;
At each step it squelched,
The warrior’s blood trickling.
Yet if the fierce woman would not walk,
Her flylike soul cried out.
“The dear bird, a wild duck,
Flies over the plain without turning back,” she said.
Having seen so much, Kanykey
Went lamenting and weeping,
“For the child born from my womb,” she said.
“The wretched bird called the kite
Swoops in flight over the plain,” she said.
Your wretched mother Kanykey
Was wasting away as she went,
“For the child born from my belly,” she said.
“My ocean, my lord, would that you had not died!
Would that this poor soul had not known wandering!
Humiliation such as this,
O God, if you create living souls,
Never again grant it to your servant!
Alas, my forehead bone was crooked:
After my king passed away,
The days I was to see were meager!
The hair at my nape was wool:
When the sultan passed away,
My lot was to see days of calamity.
The Gray Belt left by the magnanimous one
I fasten at my waist as his gift.
To the city of my father Karakan,
O God, how shall I go wandering?!
My dear, long thick hair,
How shall I braid it down over my hips?
My lord Manas, would that you had not died!
To my father, the ruling khan’s city,
As though visiting my birth family,
Staggering in mourning,
How shall I look upon his face this year?!
To great Bukhara, the ruined city,
O God, shall I reach a corner and settle?
Fierce Ubaker, may you fare ill!
Bereft of my great one,
I, unfortunate and tormented,
Shall I earn the name of wanderer?
Revealing my widow’s plight,
To my father Karakan’s city,
With my aged mother Chyyyrdy
Riding upon my moonlike back,
